needs_redesign.capability: CONTRIBUTING — required CI checks and fork-PR handling
needs_redesign.why: Five required checks map to different tools, and one maps to nothing. Semgrep's p/kotlin and p/java rulesets provide ZERO Swift coverage — porting the Security Scan Gate by name would produce a permanently green gate that scans nothing, which is worse than having no gate. The Android Gate's Gradle build becomes xcodebuild on macOS runners at roughly a 10× minute multiplier, so the paths-filter fan-out stops being an optimisation and becomes a cost requirement. Fork PRs also stop being merely a contribution path and become the primary distribution mechanism.
options: SwiftLint and SwiftFormat only
A real Swift security stack satisfying the Android gates in substance
Accept reduced security coverage and document it
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2, satisfying substance rather than tool names. Concretely: **iOS Gate** — xcodebuild test on an iOS Simulator destination and a watchOS Simulator destination plus xcodebuild build for both schemes, gated behind a dorny/paths-filter fan-out with an always-running aggregation job that fails closed, exactly as android.yml does. **Security Scan Gate** — Semgrep p/swift and p/secrets (Semgrep's own registry supports Swift; the Kotlin/Java packs do not apply at all), plus swiftlint --strict with a security-focused custom rule set, plus a canary assertion that the scan actually parsed Swift files rather than reporting zero targets. **Dependency Scan Gate** — OSV-Scanner over the committed Package.resolved (OSV parses SwiftPM manifests), same fail-on-any-known-CVE policy, same osv-scanner.toml suppression file requiring a written reason and an ignoreUntil. **Attribution Check** — unchanged, including its pull_request_target design that never checks out PR code. **Workflow Lint / Workflow Security** — actionlint + shellcheck + SHA-pin guard, and zizmor at Medium+ with a rationale-per-entry allowlist and never a lowered threshold; both are language-agnostic and port as-is. Add an **Attribution Gate** for the license generator. Newly needed and absent from Android: an IPA/entitlements posture check is the analogue of the MobSF decision the Android repo declined — and its own stated revisit trigger (a write surface, or store distribution) does not fire here, so declining it again is consistent. Fork PRs must run every required check with no maintainer action.

needs_redesign.capability: ADR 0002 / ADR 0003 — tolerant reader and contract-drift strategy
needs_redesign.why: The client half of ADR 0002 is stated in terms of Moshi. Swift Codable matches Moshi on the property that matters (unknown keys ignored, so additive backend drift is tolerated) but differs elsewhere: no @Json rename annotation (CodingKeys instead), stricter type-mismatch behavior, and default-value semantics that are expressed differently. ADR 0003's ContractSmokeTest and its field-presence coupling must be rebuilt in XCTest.
options: Re-adopt both ADRs verbatim with a short Swift addendum
Write new iOS ADRs 0002 and 0003 keeping both decisions and all the reasoning
Build the full DTO↔OpenAPI structural diff that Android ADR 0003 deliberately declined
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2. Keep both decisions and their reasoning intact. From ADR 0002 preserve: the backend's tolerant-reader behavior (legacy-value migration before validation, loose-typed pass-through fields) IS the cross-cadence compatibility mechanism, and only TWO directions are established — older app → newer backend, and newer backend → older app; newer app → older backend is NOT proven and is handled defensively per ADR 0001. From ADR 0003 preserve the proportionality argument for a smoke test over a structural diff, and the pin-refresh procedure: copy the platform's openapi.json byte-for-byte and bump contract/CONTRACT_VERSION. Reject option 3 for the same reason Android did. Critically, carry the KNOWN BLIND SPOT forward unchanged, because Swift behaves identically here: removal of a nullable or defaulted consumed field decodes to nil silently and is NOT caught by round-trip parsing. The known instance — Nightscout pump_events[].units, where a null DROPS the event and UNDERSTATES IoB — must stay covered by explicit field-presence coupling against the pinned spec, and the rule stands that any new nullable consumed field whose absence would silently degrade a safety surface must be added to that coupling.

needs_redesign.capability: README device verification table (authoritative safety status)
needs_redesign.why: The medical disclaimer defers to this table as the authoritative per-device safety status, so it cannot be inherited across platforms — an iOS BLE stack is a different code path than the Android one, and a 'Verified' claim carried over would be a false safety claim about software nobody has run. iOS verification also starts materially worse: the team has one Tandem t:slim X2 on one maintainer's iPhone, no Medtronic hardware, no Tandem Mobi, and no Simulator path for any BLE at all.
options: Publish an independent iOS table with honest per-device status from day one
Omit devices nobody can verify until a tester exists
Inherit the Android statuses with a blanket iOS caveat
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1, and option 3 is not acceptable at any point. Add a column the Android table lacks — 'validated on iOS hardware by / on date' — and make a named tester plus a date the precondition for any status better than 'unverified'. Expected v1 state: Tandem t:slim X2 verified on iOS hardware by the named maintainer; Tandem Mobi protocol-compatible, unverified on hardware, no tester; Medtronic MiniMed 680G/770G/780G beta, read-only, unverified on hardware, no tester. Port unchanged alongside it: the pre-Overview IMPORTANT SAFETY WARNING blockquote, the `## Disclaimer` section (use at your own risk, not FDA-approved, does not control any medical device, AI can be wrong, verify dosing and carb-ratio and correction-factor suggestions with your care team), and the `## License` section — still the ONLY README section packaged into the app, so its no-later-`## `-heading constraint and its exact content (project name and description, Copyright (C) 2026 Josh Engelbrecht, GPL-3.0 with SPDX GPL-3.0-only and no or-later, pointers to LICENSE and the SPDX header policy, inbound=outbound, the GPL no-warranty paragraph) are all still test-enforced.

needs_redesign.capability: PRIVACY.md — the outbound-connection and storage claims
needs_redesign.why: Three of the four documented outbound connections change and one disappears entirely. The Wear OS Data Layer over Google Play Services becomes WatchConnectivity, which removes a third party from the path. The GitHub release-API 'Check for updates' connection has no iOS install path behind it. EncryptedSharedPreferences and the SQLCipher-encrypted Room database become Keychain and Data Protection. And a user-built app has no App Store privacy label and no Apple review of any of these claims.
options: Restate the same claim structure with iOS transports and storage primitives
Restate plus add an App-Store-style disclosure table even though no store listing exists
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1; option 2 implies a review that never happens. New claim set, keeping the same 'exactly N outbound connections, all user-chosen' structure: (1) the pump over BLE, direct and local — unchanged; (2) the self-hosted backend if configured, with the backend-optional local mode still fully functional (local BLE monitoring, on-device storage, local threshold alerts, zero network calls) — unchanged and load-bearing; (3) the watch over WatchConnectivity, an Apple-local transport carrying glucose, trend, IoB and alerts only, never credentials — and state explicitly that unlike Wear OS this involves no third-party services transport; (4) the GitHub release check becomes at most an explicitly user-initiated version comparison with no download, and Apple/TestFlight replaces it as the update mechanism, seeing the user's own Apple ID and install metadata under the user's OWN developer account. Storage claims: credentials in the Keychain with a device-only after-first-unlock accessibility class; glucose and insulin in an encrypted store under a file-protection class no weaker than complete-until-first-user-authentication; the watch keeping only a small rolling render cache in app-private storage, no credentials, and no network requests. Keep: no telemetry, no analytics, the platform repo's privacy page as canonical on conflict, and reporting through the SECURITY.md channels. Add the honest new sentence: these claims describe the source at a given tag; a user's own build is their own.

needs_redesign.why: Two clauses become factually false and one becomes materially stricter. 'Project-owned unofficial builds are sideloaded from this repo's Releases page only; an APK from anywhere else is not covered' has no iOS analogue — there IS no project-owned build, and every binary is user-built. And Critical Warning #4's alert-delivery dependency list (BLE holding, Android scheduling background work, watch in range, phone charged) is Android-specific and understates iOS's constraints.
options: Rewrite the two affected clauses and leave the rest
Rewrite plus obtain legal review of the every-user-is-the-builder posture before publishing fork-and-build instructions
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2 — see questions_for_pm; the Android disclaimer already reserves 'users become the manufacturer of their own personal medical device' for fork users following the Loop/AndroidAPS precedent, and on iOS that description arguably fits every user. Warning #4's iOS list must be strictly MORE conservative and must never be weakened: alerts depend on the BLE link holding, iOS not having suspended or terminated the app, Core Bluetooth state restoration successfully relaunching it, Background App Refresh being enabled, Low Power Mode being off, the user's Focus / Do Not Disturb / notification-summary / per-app mute settings, and the watch being in range — and a user-built non-App-Store app cannot use the Critical Alerts entitlement, so notifications are silenceable by ordinary device settings. The supplement-not-replacement claim and the instruction to keep the pump's and CGM's own alerts enabled stay verbatim and become more load-bearing. Preserve unchanged: the five Critical Warnings' structure, the AI limitation list (hallucination, misinterpreting glucose data, outdated guidance, missing context), all AI content labelled suggestions not medical advice, the third-party-fork refusal, the untested-device clause (protocol compatibility does not guarantee correct operation; verify IoB, glucose and basal against the manufacturer's official app; the README table is authoritative), the caps-then-GPL-§15/16/17 liability grounding, the EU/UK/Australia jurisdictional note, and the statement that the PRIMARY risk mitigation is the monitoring-only design rather than the disclaimer.

needs_redesign.capability: docs/dev/ section — the eight developer-reference pages
needs_redesign.why: Five of the eight document Android, Gradle and GitHub-Actions mechanics with materially different iOS answers; two need renaming to match the new architecture; one ports with new globs. The section shape, frontmatter contract and curated non-alphabetical order all survive — the contents do not.
options: Re-author page by page keeping the section structure
Collapse into fewer, longer pages
Defer the section until after v1
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1; the section is how a maintainer reproduces every gate, and deferring it strands the CI subsystem. Page mapping: instrumented-tests-ci → XCUITest on Simulator destinations, PLUS an explicit statement of the hardware-test gap, since Core Bluetooth does not exist in the Simulator and no CI runner can exercise BLE. security-testing → the Swift gate stack with its own honest 'kept vs dropped vs newly-needed' table (kept: SAST, dependency CVE, secret scanning, workflow hardening; dropped: everything targeting a running server; newly needed: a Swift-capable SAST, since the Kotlin/Java packs cover nothing here). dependency-updates → Renovate's SwiftPM support over Package.swift and Package.resolved, with the same Tier-A/Tier-B auto-merge policy and the same note about why a lockfile-equivalent must be committed for the CVE gate to have anything to scan. release-and-promotion → the develop→main promotion, release-please versioning, changelog PR and sync-back all survive; what changes is that the release produces a TAG and no binary artifact. signing-and-secrets → per-fork Apple credentials, above. plugin-architecture → driver-architecture for compile-time SwiftPM targets. wear-os-architecture → watch-architecture (phone app plus watch app, WatchConnectivity, WidgetKit complications, Smart Stack). spdx-header-policy → ports with new globs. ADD one page the Android repo has no need for: fork-and-build.md, the maintainer-side reference for the per-user TestFlight pipeline, its secret contract, and its failure modes.

impossible.capability: A project-published, project-signed installable binary (app-release.apk from the topmost non-pre-release, and the dev-latest debug pre-release)
impossible.why: Apple permits installation only via the App Store, TestFlight, ad-hoc or enterprise provisioning bound to a specific team and enumerated devices, or a development build signed for a registered device. There is no signed-artifact-on-a-releases-page model at any tier. A TestFlight group belongs to exactly one App Store Connect team, external testing requires Apple's Beta App Review, and the project has deliberately chosen no App Store listing — which is also what keeps GPL-3.0-only workable, since the App Store's terms conflict with GPLv3's anti-DRM and installation-information provisions. The Android two-track model (signed release APK for users, debug APK from a dev-latest pre-release for developers) therefore has no counterpart on either track.
impossible.closest_alternative: The fork-and-build model already chosen, following Loop and xDrip4iOS: the project publishes SOURCE at signed git tags, and each user's own fork runs a GitHub Actions workflow that signs with the user's own Apple Developer account and uploads to that user's own internal TestFlight (up to 100 internal testers, 90-day build expiry, no Beta App Review). The docs replace 'download the topmost release without the Pre-release label' with 'run your fork's release workflow against tag vX.Y.Z', and the release-vs-dev-latest distinction becomes tag-build vs main-branch-build in the user's own fork. This is also strictly stronger for GPL compliance: every user provably holds the corresponding source and their own signing key.

impossible.capability: Custom watch face (the watchface module, Watch Face Format, and the phone-pushes-the-face Watch Face Push API)
impossible.why: watchOS has no third-party watch faces. Apple exposes no public API to author, install, push, or replace a face; there is no format analogous to Watch Face Format, no counterpart to androidx.wear.watchface:watchface-push, and no counterpart to the Wear OS 5 versus 6 branching the Android page documents. This is not a permissions or entitlement gap that a request could close — the surface does not exist for developers at any tier. Everything downstream of it disappears too: the separate watchface-release.apk, the two-variant watchface build (digitalFull and analogMechanical) that the Android attribution generator resolves as two of its four AttributionSources, and the entire ADB-install-the-face workflow.
impossible.closest_alternative: WidgetKit complications in the accessoryCircular, accessoryCorner, accessoryRectangular and accessoryInline families, which the user manually adds to an Apple-provided face, plus a Smart Stack widget with relevance hinting, plus the full watch app for the richer view. Every data element the Android face renders is preserved — glucose, trend arrow up/down/flat, IoB, time — as is the ~5-minute glucose-interval cadence, the '--' staleness threshold, and the strictly read-only posture. What is genuinely lost: control of the whole face surface, any guarantee of placement (the user chooses the face and the slot), and guaranteed refresh cadence (complication timeline reloads are budgeted by the system). The docs must state all three losses rather than implying parity.

impossible.capability: ADB-based install, sideloading, and the separate watch-app install workflow
impossible.why: iOS and watchOS expose no adb equivalent, no unknown-sources permission, no Developer Options unlocked by tapping Build number seven times, no Debug over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth pairing that surfaces an <ip>:<port>, and no way to install an app onto the watch independently of the phone. INSTALL_FAILED_USER_RESTRICTED, the work-device policy-block case, and the 'Wear OS forbids APK download from the watch browser' constraint the Android docs call the hardest step in the whole product all have no analogue.
impossible.closest_alternative: The watch app is embedded in the phone app's bundle and installs automatically when the user installs the phone app from TestFlight. The entire Android watch-install page collapses to 'accept the TestFlight invite, then long-press your watch face, tap Edit, and add the GlycemicGPT complication.' This is a strict simplification and the docs should say so explicitly — the single hardest documented step in the Android product is removed. For developers, Xcode's Devices and Simulators window installs directly to a connected iPhone, which is the nearest thing to the adb path and belongs in the developer section, not the user-facing install page.

impossible.capability: In-app 'Check for updates' that downloads and installs a newer build
impossible.why: iOS forbids an application from fetching and executing code that was not signed into its bundle; there is no counterpart to downloading an APK from github.com or objects.githubusercontent.com and installing it, and no in-place upgrade path an app can trigger. The Android page's related claims — no auto-update, a stale-version banner, and an in-place APK upgrade that preserves settings, login and pairing — are all either impossible or inverted, since TestFlight updates automatically and installs are managed by the system.
impossible.closest_alternative: TestFlight delivers updates automatically once the user's fork uploads a new build. The app may at most compare its own embedded source tag against the upstream repository's latest tag and display a non-actionable banner: 'a newer version is available — re-run your fork's build workflow.' PRIVACY.md's fourth outbound connection changes character accordingly: it stops being an install path and becomes, at most, an explicitly user-initiated version check that downloads nothing. The app should additionally surface its own TestFlight build expiry date, which is a real staleness signal the Android app has no need for.

impossible.capability: Guaranteed or undismissable alert delivery, and the Critical Alerts entitlement
impossible.why: UNNotificationInterruptionLevel.critical requires the com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts entitlement, which Apple grants only by reviewed request against a specific App Store Connect app record, and which is not realistically obtainable for a user-built, non-App-Store, explicitly-unofficial app — and every user's fork would need its own grant against its own bundle ID. Separately, iOS has no foreground service: there is no mechanism to keep a process alive indefinitely. BGTaskScheduler runs at the system's discretion and cannot guarantee a 5-minute cadence; Core Bluetooth background delivery is event-driven only; and CBCentralManager state restoration hands back the peripherals and scan state but explicitly cannot resume arbitrary work, so an app relaunched into the background must reconstruct its own context and may be terminated again. Android's battery-optimization exemption, which the Android docs present as the fix for a dropping background link, has no user-facing counterpart at all.
impossible.closest_alternative: A layered, honestly-described alerting posture: .timeSensitive interruption level (breaks through Focus, but not through the user muting the app or disabling its notifications), a Live Activity while a pump session is active so glucose stays visible on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island, an audible in-app alarm while the app is foreground, the bluetooth-central background mode with CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey so the OS relaunches the app on peripheral events, and a watch-side complication as an independent surface. MEDICAL-DISCLAIMER Critical Warning #4 must be made STRICTER on iOS and must never be weakened: the supplement-not-replacement framing and the instruction to keep the pump's and CGM's own alerts enabled are the actual safety mechanism, and the docs must not imply the app can be relied on as a primary alarm.

impossible.why: iOS forbids loading executable code that was not signed into the app bundle at build time. There is no counterpart to DexClassLoader, dlopen of a downloaded binary is rejected at load, and any mechanism that fetched and executed a driver at runtime would be both a signing violation and a code-injection surface in an app handling glucose data. This is a settled platform rule, not a v1 scope cut, and is already reflected in the product decision that drivers are compile-time-linked Swift modules.
impossible.closest_alternative: Every driver is a compile-time-linked SwiftPM target under Sources/Drivers/. The CONTRIBUTING step describing runtime-loaded plugins as a separate advanced path not compiled into official builds is DELETED rather than adapted, and the docs should state the tradeoff plainly: adding a new device on iOS requires a source change, a merged PR, and a rebuild by each user, not a dropped-in plugin. One mitigating property of the distribution model is that a user who wants an unmerged driver can already build their own fork with it — which is the same affordance the plugin path provided, arrived at differently.

impossible.capability: Battery-optimization exemption as a documented, user-performable action
impossible.why: iOS has no per-app battery-optimization allowlist, no Samsung-style 'Sleeping apps' list, and no user-facing setting that grants an app durable background execution. The Android docs make this exemption a prerequisite in two separate published pages (install.md and cant-pair-pump.md) because without it the background pump link drops; there is nothing on iOS a user can toggle that provides the equivalent guarantee. The related '<5%/day battery impact' figure is an Android measurement of an Android background model and cannot be carried over.
impossible.closest_alternative: Document what the user CAN control and be explicit about what they cannot: enable Background App Refresh for the app, keep Low Power Mode off, and do not swipe the app away in the app switcher (which suspends Core Bluetooth state restoration until the next manual launch, and is therefore the exact opposite of the Android 'force-stop then reopen' remedy). Pair this with an in-app diagnostics screen surfacing CBManagerState, Bluetooth authorization, Background App Refresh status, Low Power Mode and a last-seen-advertisement timestamp, since iOS hides all of it. Replace the battery figure with a measured iOS number gathered on the maintainer's hardware, or publish none at all — do not inherit the Android one.

ios_requirements: The published docs tree must use one _meta.json per section directory with the schema {"title": string, "pages": [string]}, entries as basenames without extension, the array order as the rendered nav order, and no root docs/_meta.json.

CI must fail a documentation PR when a page under a section directory lacks title: or description: frontmatter, is present on disk but absent from its section's pages array, or is listed in a pages array but absent from disk.
CI must fail a documentation PR containing an internal link that resolves to nothing, evaluated against the merged multi-repo website namespace rather than this repo alone.
iOS documentation pages must not share page basenames with the Android repository's pages; platform-specific content must live in platform-scoped section directories.

A push to main touching docs/** must dispatch a docs-updated repository event to the website repo using a GitHub App token minted with no GITHUB_TOKEN scopes, with a manual re-dispatch available to force a rebuild after a failed run.

A user must be able to go from a fresh fork to a working app on their own iPhone using only the published build-and-install page: Apple Developer Program membership, an App Store Connect API key, a documented set of repository secrets, one workflow run, and a TestFlight invite.
The build-and-install page must state the 90-day TestFlight build expiry and the exact action required to refresh it before it lapses.
The app must surface its own build expiry date and source tag in Settings so a user can see staleness without consulting TestFlight.

The project must never hold, request, or transmit any user's Apple signing material; all signing credentials must live only in the user's own fork's repository secrets, and a leaked credential must compromise only that user's own Apple account.
The build pipeline must produce a signed, TestFlight-uploadable build from a fork in which no project-owned secret is present.

The app must ship an in-app license viewer reachable from Settings, with distinct Loading, Loaded and Unavailable states, full text selection, preserved scroll position across rotation and scene restoration, and no network requirement.

The license viewer must display, in order: the project license notice, the third-party source-lineage document, one section per redistributed-component license family, the bundled license texts, and the complete GPL-3.0 text.

License texts and the GPL must be rendered as plain text and never as markdown, and repository-relative links in any displayed document must be reduced to their label text while scheme-bearing targets including mailto: are preserved.

The shipped license assets must be generated from the resolved dependency graph on every build, covering every target that ships in a binary including the watch app and any widget extension; committed pre-generated assets must not be accepted.

The build must fail — not warn — when the resolved component list is empty, when a component has no SPDX identifier and no classification entry, when a license family has no bundled text file, when a whole-file source document is blank, or when README.md has no `## License` heading.

The build must fail when a dependency's license is not on the checked-in allowlist; EPL-1.0 must not be allowlisted, and an EPL-licensed transitive must be excluded at the dependency with a test proving the affected feature still works.
Every per-package license exception must be pinned to an exact version and carry a written reason, so a version bump re-raises the judgement rather than inheriting it.

An automated test must assert byte-for-byte equality between each shipped license asset and its on-disk source, must fail on any component-document heading outside the declared SPDX and non-SPDX heading sets, and must assert a named stable witness component and a non-empty upstream-notices block.
Editing README.md, LICENSE, docs/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md or docs/licenses/** must invalidate cached test results and trigger the application build gate; every other docs change must skip it.

Every in-scope Swift, shell and workflow file must carry the SPDX identifier GPL-3.0-only and the copyright line naming the individual holder; ported upstream trees must be excluded from that stamp and must instead carry their own upstream notice in-file, specifically including Apache-2.0 and the Particle Industries copyright on the EC-JPAKE source.

A published acknowledgments page must state, per upstream project, whether its code was studied and reimplemented or copied and ported, and must name the license and any explicit relicensing permission relied on.
A repo-internal, unpublished provenance record must state, per Swift module, which Android source file and commit it derives from, or that it was reimplemented from protocol documentation only.

The published medical disclaimer must state that no therapeutic write surface exists anywhere, that no capability protocol exposes an insulin-delivery primitive, and that permitted device-management operations are exactly CGM calibration, BLE pair and unpair, and connect and disconnect.

The published alert-delivery warning must enumerate every iOS-specific condition that alert delivery depends on, and must state that app alerts are a supplement to the pump's and CGM's own alerts, never a replacement, and that device alerts must remain enabled.
No product surface may claim that alerts are guaranteed, undismissable, or capable of overriding the user's own notification, Focus, or mute settings.

The published README must carry an iOS-specific per-device verification table including a 'validated on iOS hardware by / on date' column, and the medical disclaimer must defer to that table; no device status may be inherited from the Android table.

Onboarding must present a safety-acknowledgement page that cannot be skipped or swiped past, requires an explicit 'I Understand' action, and shows all five disclaimer cards including the warning never to calculate an insulin dose from a photo carb estimate; users who previously completed onboarding must be re-run through it whenever the disclaimer changes.

The published privacy document must enumerate every outbound connection by name, state that each is user-chosen, and state that with no backend configured the app performs local BLE monitoring, on-device storage and local threshold alerts with zero network calls.

Any error-monitoring integration must compile with an empty DSN in every pipeline-produced build, must fail the build outright if a DSN reaches CI, and must transmit no glucose, health, identifier, credential, device-serial, database or HTTP-body data.

Credentials must be stored in the Keychain with a device-only, after-first-unlock accessibility class; health data must be stored under a file-protection class no weaker than complete-until-first-user-authentication; the watch must store no credentials and must make no network requests.

Security reports must have two private channels and no public issue path, and the policy must classify a BLE parsing defect that produces a wrong glucose, IoB or dosing-history value as a report for that channel rather than an ordinary bug.
The security policy must pre-decline, in writing, any report proposing that the absent therapeutic-write capability be added.
Every commit must carry a valid Signed-off-by trailer, enforced server-side with no exemption tier and a one-remediation-commit allowance, with no CLA and no relicensing rights granted.

Pull requests must be blocked when AI attribution appears in commit trailers, in added source lines, or in the PR description, using the same three-severity ladder and anchored bot allowlist, with .swift included in the scanned extension set.

Required pull-request checks must cover, in substance: build and unit tests on iOS and watchOS Simulator destinations, Swift static analysis with security rules that demonstrably parse Swift, dependency CVE scanning over the committed dependency lockfile, license attribution generation, AI attribution, and workflow lint plus workflow security scanning.
The Swift static-analysis gate must fail closed if the scanner errors, and must fail if it reports zero scanned Swift files.
Fork-originated pull requests must run every required check with no maintainer action, and no privileged check may check out pull-request code into a writable working tree.

A driver contribution must declare which capability protocols it implements from the read-only set, must discard and log any reading outside SafetyLimits rather than returning, emitting or persisting it, must include parsing and limits-validation tests, and must name who will validate it on physical hardware.

The three cross-repo safety constants — 18.0156, the 20 to 500 mg/dL validity bound, and the 1199145600-second Tandem epoch offset — must each exist as exactly one Swift definition, be documented on a single contract page listing every consuming site, and be guarded by a test that fails when a duplicate or divergent definition appears.

Glucose must be stored and compared in mg/dL at every persisted field, bound, threshold, alert comparison, dedup key and safety check; mmol/L must exist only at display and input boundaries, converted with the single sanctioned factor and rounded last.

The app must vendor a monotonic CONTRACT_VERSION integer and a byte-for-byte-pinned OpenAPI document, must treat an absent or unparseable backend compatibility signal as absent rather than compatible, must fail open on read and monitoring paths with a one-time dismissible warning, and must refuse any future safety-critical write when backend compatibility is unknown.

Contract tests must assert the presence of every nullable consumed field whose absence would silently degrade a safety surface, explicitly including the Nightscout pump-event insulin-units field whose absence drops the event and understates IoB.

The repository must ship a code of conduct with a reporting address distinct from the security address, a governance stub delegating to the organisation-level document, a CODEOWNERS file requiring lead review on driver, workflow, policy and release-configuration changes, and pull-request and issue templates including a hardware-validation field.

Documentation-only pull requests must receive a docs label and a Documentation changelog section without triggering the application build gate, except when they touch one of the four license-bearing paths.

The watch setup page must state that the watch app installs automatically with the phone app, that a complication must be added manually to an Apple-provided face, and that watchOS provides no custom watch face and no equivalent of pushing a face from the phone.

An in-app diagnostics surface must report Bluetooth manager state and authorization, Background App Refresh status, Low Power Mode, and the last-seen-advertisement and last-successful-pump-read timestamps, so troubleshooting documentation has something actionable to point at.

risks.risk: The license asset pipeline has no off-the-shelf Swift equivalent with the Android version's fail-closed behavior. LicensePlist and similar tools generate files but warn rather than fail on an unclassified component, an empty component list, or a missing license text — so a naive tool swap silently converts five build-breaking guarantees into zero.
risks.mitigation: Build the generator as a small in-repo Swift executable and write the five failure modes as tests of the generator itself before the first TestFlight build exists. Port LicenseAssetsTest as an XCTest against the built bundle on day one, so no build path can ever ship a blank or stale license screen.

risks.risk: Because every user builds and signs their own binary, the project cannot verify what any installed build actually contains. A user could compile in a Sentry DSN, add a therapeutic write, or edit the disclaimer, and the result would still look and be called GlycemicGPT. Every legal claim in PRIVACY.md and MEDICAL-DISCLAIMER.md is a claim about source, not about the binary anyone is running.
risks.mitigation: State the boundary explicitly in both documents: these claims describe the source at tag vX.Y.Z; your build is yours. Keep the CI DSN-rejection check so the upstream pipeline itself cannot produce a telemetry build, keep the no-write-surface assertions in the CodeRabbit gate and the capability protocol definitions, and publish which claims are architecturally enforced versus prose.

risks.risk: Docs namespace collision. The website merges this repo's docs with the platform repo's; adding iOS produces duplicate basenames (install, cant-pair-pump, connecting-medtronic-pump) and silently wrong link resolution, and nothing in any repo detects it because there is no link checker and no cross-repo validation anywhere today.
risks.mitigation: Platform-scoped section directories so no basename is ever shared, a small stable shared-anchor set owned by the platform repo, and a link check that runs in the website repo against the merged tree. Pick one canonical org/slug before copying any absolute link forward — the Android policy docs currently carry six inconsistent slugs.

risks.risk: Semgrep's p/kotlin and p/java rulesets provide zero Swift coverage, so a name-for-name port of the Security Scan Gate would produce a permanently green required check that scans nothing — strictly worse than having no gate, because it manufactures false assurance for a health-data app.
risks.mitigation: Name the substitute stack explicitly in docs/dev/security-testing.md — Semgrep p/swift and p/secrets, swiftlint --strict with security rules, OSV-Scanner over Package.resolved — and add a canary step asserting the scan actually parsed a non-zero number of Swift files. Keep the existing fail-closed-on-scanner-error logic and the non-blocking unparseable-file warning, both of which port as-is.

risks.risk: The alert-delivery claim is the highest-consequence prose in the repository, and iOS is materially weaker than Android on every dependency it names. An inherited Critical Warning #4 would overstate reliability for a user who reasonably treats the app as a glucose alarm.
risks.mitigation: Rewrite Warning #4 before any hardware testing begins, not after, so no tester ever reads the Android version. Enumerate every iOS condition including Focus, per-app mute, state restoration and app-switcher dismissal, and add a CodeRabbit Medical Safety rule that flags any diff weakening alerting language in the disclaimer or the app.

risks.risk: No one on the team has Medtronic hardware or a Tandem Mobi, the lead has no iPhone and no Apple Watch, and Core Bluetooth does not exist in the Simulator. The iOS device verification table therefore starts nearly empty, and the medical disclaimer defers to that table as authoritative safety status.
risks.mitigation: Publish the table with honest empty statuses from the first commit, make a named tester and a date the precondition for any status better than 'unverified on hardware', and build a simulated driver so parser correctness and safety-limit rejection stay testable in CI without hardware. Add the hardware-validation field to the PR template so the gap is visible on every driver change.

risks.risk: macOS runners cost roughly ten times Linux minutes, and the Android repo's Security Scan Gate runs unconditionally on every PR by design so the required status always reports. Naively porting that pattern to xcodebuild makes the build gate expensive enough that a maintainer is tempted to weaken it.
risks.mitigation: Keep the paths-filter fan-out plus always-running aggregation-gate pattern for the build and test gate so the required check still reports on skipped runs, and run the cheap Linux-native gates — attribution check, workflow lint, workflow security, dependency scan, Swift SAST — unfiltered on every PR.

risks.risk: TestFlight builds expire after 90 days. A user who stops rebuilding loses a working glucose monitor, and unlike a sideloaded APK there is no version that simply keeps running.
risks.mitigation: Document the expiry prominently on the install page rather than in a footnote, surface the build's own expiry date in the app's Settings screen with escalating prominence as it approaches, and consider a scheduled workflow in the fork template that rebuilds automatically.

risks.risk: CBPeripheralManager drops the advertised local name once the app is backgrounded, and the Medtronic pairing flow depends on the phone advertising as exactly 'Mobile 000001'. Publishing the Android page's 'pairing is remembered; reconnect is automatic when back in range' claim unchanged would be wrong for initial discovery.
risks.mitigation: Document Medtronic pairing as an explicitly foreground, screen-on operation and reconnection as best-effort in background; verify the split on hardware before publishing the page; and add a named error string for the Bluetooth-permission and background-advertising cases alongside the five existing ones.

risks.risk: The Android repo instructs contributors to fill out a PR template that does not exist, references docs/dev/monorepo-port-ledger.md which does not exist, and carries a ci.yml whose own comment claims it is the only workflow while eighteen others exist. Copying CONTRIBUTING and the workflow set forward carries all three defects into a new repository.
risks.mitigation: Ship .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md and issue forms in the first commit, replace the port-ledger reference with the provenance record that actually exists, and audit every workflow header comment for inherited stale claims before the repo goes public.

risks.risk: GPL-3.0-only combined with a per-user Apple Developer account places each user in the position of builder, signer and distributor-to-self. The Android disclaimer reserves the 'user becomes the manufacturer of their own personal medical device' framing for third-party forks that add device control; on iOS that description may fit every single user of the software.
risks.mitigation: Obtain legal review of the disclaimer's distribution and manufacturer clauses before the fork-and-build instructions are published, not after the first user builds. Until reviewed, the install page should state the builder relationship factually without asserting a legal conclusion in either direction.

questions_for_pm: On Android the project publishes a signed binary from its own Releases page, and MEDICAL-DISCLAIMER.md reserves the 'users become the manufacturer of their own personal medical device' framing (citing the Loop/AndroidAPS precedent) for third-party forks that add device control. On iOS there is no project-published build at all: every user forks the source, signs with their own Apple Developer account, and installs into their own TestFlight. Does the iOS disclaimer need counsel review on whether that framing now describes every user rather than only fork users — and if counsel says it does, does that change whether the project publishes fork-and-build instructions publicly, or only how the disclaimer is worded? This is the one determination in this subsystem that cannot be made from the Android repo, Apple's platform rules, or the stated product context, and it gates the two highest-traffic published pages (the install runbook and the medical disclaimer).
